title: Comparison and Modification
summary: Comparatives, superlatives, adjective-versus-adverb choices, and where modifiers belong in the sentence.

sections.heading: Forming Comparatives and Superlatives
sections.body:
One-syllable adjectives take `-er` and `-est`: `fast`, `faster`, `the fastest`. Adjectives of three syllables or more take `more` and `most`: `more significant`, `the most significant`. Adjectives ending in `-y` change to `-ier` and `-iest`: `easy`, `easier`, `the easiest`.

Two-syllable adjectives are the grey area. Those ending in `-y`, `-er`, `-ow` and `-le` normally take the ending (`narrower`, `simpler`, `gentler`), while the rest usually take `more` (`more useful`, `more common`, `more careful`). Several accept either form, so `clever`, `common` and `quiet` are equally correct with `-er` or with `more`. Outside the `-y` group, where `more easy` and `more happy` are not used, `more` is rarely a real error, which makes it a reasonably safe default under exam pressure.

The irregulars have to be memorised: `good` becomes `better` and `best`, `bad` becomes `worse` and `worst`, and `far` becomes `further` or `farther` and `furthest` or `farthest`.

examples.right: The revised syllabus is simpler than the one it replaced.
examples.wrong: The revised syllabus is more simple than the one it replaced.
examples.note: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -le normally take -er.

examples.right: Air quality was worse in the industrial districts.
examples.wrong: Air quality was badder in the industrial districts.
examples.note: `bad` is irregular: worse, worst.

examples.right: This is the most persuasive argument in the paper.
examples.wrong: This is the persuasivest argument in the paper.
examples.note: Three or more syllables always take most.

sections.heading: Than, As ... As, and the Double Comparative
sections.body:
A comparative is followed by **than**, not `then`. `Than` compares; `then` refers to time or consequence. The two are pronounced almost identically in connected speech, which is why the error survives into writing.

A comparison is marked once and once only. `More easier` and `most cheapest` are double comparatives: either the ending or the word `more` carries the meaning, never both.

Equality is expressed with **as ... as**, negated as `not as ... as` or `not so ... as`, and multiplied with `twice as ... as`, `three times as ... as`. Parallel change uses **the ... the**: `the more` one clause, `the more` the other, with a comma between the halves.

examples.right: The second method proved more accurate than the first.
examples.wrong: The second method proved more accurate then the first.
examples.note: Comparison takes `than`; `then` is temporal.

examples.right: Rural clinics are far more difficult to staff.
examples.wrong: Rural clinics are far more difficulter to staff.
examples.note: Never mark the comparative twice.

examples.right: The pilot study was not as conclusive as the researchers had hoped.
examples.wrong: The pilot study was not as conclusive than the researchers had hoped.
examples.note: Equality uses as ... as, even when negated.

examples.right: The larger the sample, the more reliable the estimate.
examples.wrong: Larger the sample, more reliable the estimate.
examples.note: Both halves of the parallel structure need `the`.

sections.heading: Modifying a Comparison
sections.body:
A comparative can be strengthened or softened, but not by `very`. Use **much**, **far**, **a lot**, **considerably** or **significantly** to strengthen, and **slightly**, **marginally**, **somewhat** or **a little** to soften. `Very` modifies the plain adjective only: `very expensive`, but `far more expensive`.

A superlative normally takes `the`, and the range it applies to is introduced by `in` for places and groups, and `of` for a stated set: `the busiest airport in Europe`, `the cheapest of the three options`.

The pattern **one of the + superlative + plural noun** is fixed. The noun after it is plural because the item is being placed inside a group, even though the verb that follows agrees with `one`.

examples.right: The new turbine is considerably more efficient than the old one.
examples.wrong: The new turbine is very more efficient than the old one.
examples.note: `Very` cannot modify a comparative.

examples.right: Sales rose slightly faster in the second quarter.
examples.note: `Slightly` softens the comparative without changing its form.

examples.right: Lagos is one of the fastest growing cities in the world.
examples.wrong: Lagos is one of the fastest growing city in the world.
examples.note: `One of the` is always followed by a plural noun.

examples.right: It was the least expensive of the three proposals.
examples.wrong: It was the least expensive in the three proposals.
examples.note: A stated set takes `of`, not `in`.

sections.heading: Adjective or Adverb
sections.body:
An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb. A handful of words have two forms with unrelated meanings: `hard` means with effort while **hardly** means barely, and `late` means not on time while **lately** means recently. `He works hard` and `he hardly works` are opposites.

After a linking verb the complement describes the subject, so it stays an adjective. The common linking verbs are `be`, `seem`, `appear`, `become`, `remain`, `stay`, and the perception verbs `feel`, `look`, `sound`, `taste` and `smell`. `The proposal seems reasonable` is correct; `seems reasonably` is not.

Several of these verbs can also be ordinary action verbs, and then an adverb is right: compare `the mixture smelled strange` with `she smelled the mixture cautiously`.

examples.right: The committee hardly ever meets during the summer.
examples.wrong: The committee hard ever meets during the summer.
examples.note: `Hardly` means almost never; `hard` means with effort.

examples.right: Interest in the programme has grown steadily lately.
examples.wrong: Interest in the programme has grown steadily late.
examples.note: `Lately` means recently; `late` means after the expected time.

examples.right: The water tasted fresh once the filter had been replaced.
examples.wrong: The water tasted freshly once the filter had been replaced.
examples.note: After a perception verb the complement describes the subject.

sections.heading: Adjectives Ending in -ed and -ing
sections.body:
The `-ing` participial adjective names the source of a feeling; the `-ed` form names the person who has it. A lecture is **boring**; the audience is **bored**. Saying `I am boring` states that other people find you dull.

The pairs that cause the most trouble are `interested/interesting`, `confused/confusing`, `frustrated/frustrating`, `surprised/surprising`, `tired/tiring` and `worried/worrying`. Arabic does not distinguish these with two separate participles, and this is one of the most persistent B2 slips: the rule is understood but the wrong form still appears under time pressure.

A quick test: if the word can be replaced by `causing that feeling`, use `-ing`; if it can be replaced by `feeling that way`, use `-ed`.

examples.right: The results were surprising, and the reviewers were surprised by them.
examples.note: The same event is -ing; the people who react are -ed.

examples.right: Many participants found the instructions confusing.
examples.wrong: Many participants found the instructions confused.
examples.note: The instructions cause the confusion; they do not feel it.

examples.right: She was frustrated by the delay.
examples.wrong: She was frustrating by the delay.
examples.note: The subject experiences the feeling, so -ed.

sections.heading: Where Modifiers Go
sections.body:
Adverbs of frequency (`always`, `often`, `rarely`, `never`) go before a main verb but after `be` and after the first auxiliary: `she rarely comments`, `she is rarely present`, `she has rarely commented`. Adverbs of manner (`carefully`, `quickly`) usually follow the verb or its object, never between the verb and its object: `read the report carefully`, not `read carefully the report`. Adverbs of degree (`completely`, `almost`, `entirely`) go immediately before the word they intensify.

When several adjectives precede a noun, English follows a fixed order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. `A small old wooden desk` is natural; any other order sounds wrong even though nothing else has changed.

Two or more adjectives of the same type are separated by commas; adjectives of different types are not.

examples.right: The department has never seriously questioned the methodology.
examples.wrong: The department has seriously never questioned the methodology.
examples.note: The frequency adverb follows the first auxiliary.

examples.right: The panel reviewed the application carefully.
examples.wrong: The panel reviewed carefully the application.
examples.note: A manner adverb does not separate the verb from its object.

examples.right: They restored a large nineteenth-century brick warehouse.
examples.wrong: They restored a brick nineteenth-century large warehouse.
examples.note: Size precedes age, which precedes material.

slips: Writing `then` where a comparison needs `than`; if the sentence compares two things, the word is `than`.
Marking the comparative twice, as in `more easier`; choose the ending or `more`, never both.
Using `very` before a comparative; strengthen it with `much`, `far` or `considerably` instead.
Following `one of the` with a singular noun; the noun is always plural, as in `one of the largest cities`.
Confusing `-ed` and `-ing` adjectives, so that `the topic is interested` appears in place of `interesting`.
Putting a manner adverb between the verb and its object, as in `explained clearly the results`.

questions.prompt: The revised timetable is ___ the original one.
questions.explain: `Simple` ends in -le, so it takes -er, and a comparison is completed by `than`. `More simpler` marks the comparative twice, and `then` is temporal, not comparative.

questions.prompt: Air quality this winter was ___ than it was last year, despite the new restrictions.
questions.explain: `Bad` is irregular: worse, worst. There is no form `badder`, and `more bad` is not used of quality.

questions.prompt: The second trial was not ___ the first, so the team ran it again.
questions.explain: Equality, including negated equality, is expressed with `as ... as`. A comparative structure with `than` requires a comparative form such as `less conclusive than`.

questions.prompt: The advisory board ___ ever meets more than twice a year.
questions.explain: `Hardly ever` means almost never. `Hard` is the adverb of effort, which would give the opposite sense entirely.

questions.prompt: The revised model runs ___ fast as the original, although it uses more memory.
questions.hint: express 'two times' in a comparison of equality
questions.explain: Multiples are placed in front of the `as ... as` frame: twice as fast as, three times as large as.

questions.prompt: ___ the sample, the more reliable the estimate becomes.
questions.explain: Parallel change uses `the` plus a comparative in both halves. A superlative cannot open the structure, and `large` takes -er rather than `more`.

questions.prompt: Several participants found the written instructions ___, so the researchers rewrote them.
questions.explain: The instructions cause the confusion rather than experiencing it, so the -ing form is required; `confused` would describe the participants.

questions.prompt: Even after the tank had been sealed, the water still smelled ___.
questions.explain: `Smell` here is a linking verb, so the complement is an adjective describing the water. `Strangely` would describe the manner of an action, which a linking verb does not express.

questions.prompt: The department has ___ questioned the accuracy of the figures.
questions.explain: The frequency adverb follows the first auxiliary and precedes the manner adverb. `Serious` is an adjective and cannot modify the verb at all.

questions.prompt: In the corner of the study stood a ___ wooden desk that had belonged to her grandmother.
questions.hint: small + old, in the natural English order
questions.explain: English orders premodifiers as opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, so size precedes age, which precedes the material adjective `wooden`.

questions.prompt: The second version of the software is ___ better than the first.
questions.explain: Comparatives are strengthened by `far`, `much` or `considerably`. `Very` modifies only the plain adjective, as in `very good`.

questions.prompt: Of the three routes into the city, the coastal one is ___ scenic.
questions.explain: A superlative takes `the`, and `scenic` is a two-syllable adjective that forms its superlative with `most`. `Of` signals a stated set, which is a reliable cue that a superlative is required.
